report:
**Conclusion: No — the evidence does not support arthroscopy for knee osteoarthritis.**

Your initial expectation that the answer is "yes" is contradicted by the best available evidence. Multiple high-quality randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines consistently show that arthroscopic surgery (lavage, debridement, or partial meniscectomy) provides **no meaningful benefit** over placebo surgery or conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Landmark placebo-controlled RCT (NEJM, 2002):** Moseley et al. found that arthroscopic surgery was no more effective than sham (placebo) surgery in relieving pain or improving function in patients with knee OA. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259))

2. **Cochrane review (2022):** A comprehensive review concluded that arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease (OA, degenerative meniscal tears, or both) provides no important benefit in pain or function compared with placebo or non-surgical treatment, and carries potential harms. ([https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease))

3. **BMJ rapid recommendation (2017):** An expert panel strongly recommended against arthroscopy for nearly all patients with degenerative knee disease, including those with meniscal tears and sudden symptom onset — groups previously thought to benefit. ([https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982](https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982))

4. **10-year follow-up (NEJM, 2026):** Long-term data from the FIDELITY trial confirmed no benefit from arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative meniscal tears, even at a decade of follow-up. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2516079](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2516079))

**Why might people think it works?** Patients often report feeling better after arthroscopy, but the placebo-controlled trial showed that sham surgery produces identical improvements — the benefit is attributable to placebo effects and natural disease fluctuation, not the procedure itself.

Major guidelines (NICE, AAOS, ACR) now recommend against routine arthroscopy for knee OA. The procedure continues to be performed despite this consensus, which researchers attribute to habit, financial incentives, and surgeon belief rather than evidence.
